tagline: Follow river valleys from Altavista before climbing to three Blue Ridge peaks.
intro: Route 43 bends along the Roanoke River, follows Goose Creek and climbs into Jefferson National Forest at the Peaks of Otter. Its southern section runs 39.79 miles from Altavista to the Blue Ridge Parkway, with Virginia Byway status beginning north of the US 29 bypass. The Commonwealth's byway designation identifies scenic roads that introduce travelers to alternative destinations. Bedford sits at the foot of the peaks; beyond town, the drive crosses the Otter River before ascending the mountain to the Parkway.

Travelers were staying at the peaks long before the present lodge: in 1834, Polly Wood opened an inn in her log cabin. By the 1870s, the mountain community included more than 20 families, a school, a church and the Mons Hotel. The lodge and manmade Abbott Lake arrived in 1964. The National Park Service preserves the peaks and lake as part of the Parkway.

Start in Altavista and head toward Lynch Station, where Route 43 turns southwest beside the Roanoke River. At Leesville it turns to Goose Creek; at Gillespie it joins Route 24 briefly before heading north toward Bedford on a road named Virginia Byway. Beyond Bedford, Peaks Road crosses the Otter River and ascends to the Parkway beside the Peaks of Otter Visitor Center.

moments.title: Altavista
moments.text: Altavista began at a railroad crossing planned by the people building one of the lines. In 1905, the Lane Brothers Construction Company received a contract to build railroad for the Tidewater Railway Company between Leesville and The Mansion. The company bought 2,000 acres at the junction with the Southern Railway and planned Lane's Siding. The town took the name Altavista from the Lane family farm near Charlottesville. Route 43 begins beside the crossing of Norfolk Southern's Altavista and Danville district lines, keeping that railway geography part of the road's starting point.

moments.title: Bedford
moments.text: Bedford's National D-Day Memorial connects this town at the foot of the Peaks of Otter with the Normandy landings. Nineteen of the 34 Bedford soldiers in Company A, 116th Infantry Regiment, 29th Infantry Division, were killed on D-Day. President George W. Bush dedicated the memorial on June 6, 2001. On its grounds stands a replica of the World War I memorial statue from Trévières, France. The copy preserves damage to the original statue's face caused by American artillery during World War II. Despite its national designation, the memorial is owned and operated by a nonprofit educational foundation.

moments.title: Peaks of Otter
moments.text: Three summits surround the valley of Abbott Lake: Sharp Top, Flat Top and Harkening Hill. Flat Top is the highest, despite the prominence given to Sharp Top as a hiking destination. The lake itself was created in 1964, alongside the Peaks of Otter Lodge. The National Park Service preserves the peaks and lake as part of the Blue Ridge Parkway. At Johnson Farm, the house and outbuildings retain their restored 1930s form, with gardens and a small orchard. A flat, paved trail makes a one-mile circuit of Abbott Lake below the mountains.
